So for the URL shortener, let me start with the estimate. Say 100 million new URLs a month, so roughly 40 writes per second, and a read to write ratio of 100 to 1, which gives about 4,000 QPS on redirects and maybe 20,000 at peak. For short codes, um, I'd use base62 encoding of a unique integer, and seven characters gives us 62 to the 7th, around 3.5 trillion combinations. The integer comes from a distributed ID generator, either Snowflake style IDs or a counter service backed by ZooKeeper that hands out ranges of 1,000 IDs to each app server. Hashing with MD5 and truncating is the alternative, but then you get collisions and need a retry, so I prefer the counter. For redirects, we put a CDN like CloudFront in front, then Redis as a cache-aside layer with an LRU eviction policy, targeting a 95 percent hit rate. The database is DynamoDB or Cassandra, keyed on the short code, since it's a pure key-value lookup. I'd return a 301 permanent redirect if we don't need analytics, sorry, I mean a 302 temporary redirect if we do, because browsers cache 301s and we'd lose click counts. Right, and the p99 latency target is under 50 milliseconds. We also add a TTL for expiring links and a Bloom filter to reject unknown codes cheaply.

For a rate limiter at the API gateway, I'd go with the token bucket algorithm. Um, the reason is that it allows short bursts while still enforcing a steady average rate, which is what most API customers actually want. Say each API key gets a bucket of 100 tokens that refills at 10 tokens per second. The other contender is a sliding window counter, which is more accurate than a fixed window, which has that boundary problem where you can double the limit across two windows, but it costs more memory. The state has to be shared, because we run maybe 50 gateway nodes behind a load balancer, so local in-memory counters would be wrong. So I'd keep it in Redis, one hash per key, and run a Lua script so the read, refill and decrement happen atomically. Otherwise you get race conditions. Redis Cluster shards the keys by consistent hashing, and we handle about 200,000 QPS with sub-millisecond latency, say p99 under 2 milliseconds. If Redis is down, we fail open, sorry, I mean fail open for paid tiers but fail closed for anonymous traffic. We return HTTP 429 Too Many Requests with a Retry-After header, and expose X-RateLimit-Remaining. Rules live in a config service, and we use Envoy or Kong at the gateway to enforce them.

So for the news feed, the core trade-off is fan-out on write versus fan-out on read. With fan-out on write, when someone posts, we push the post ID into each follower's feed cache, which is a Redis sorted set keyed by user and scored by timestamp. Reads are then very cheap, a single ZREVRANGE, easily under 20 milliseconds at p99. With fan-out on read we assemble the feed at request time by querying everyone you follow, which is slow and hammers the database. Normally I'd go write for most users, since the average account has maybe 200 followers. But for a celebrity with 50 million followers, a push would mean 50 million cache writes for a single post, the classic thundering herd, and the write amplification kills us. So I'd do a hybrid approach. Um, push for normal users, and for celebrities we skip fan-out and pull their posts at read time, merging them into the precomputed feed. We mark accounts above, say, a million followers as celebrities. The fan-out goes through Kafka, with worker consumers writing to the cache, so that spikes are absorbed. Posts live in Cassandra or MySQL with sharding by user ID, media in S3 behind a CDN. For ranking we use a simple ML model, sorry, I mean a lightweight ranker, applied after merging, with cursor-based pagination.

For chat, I'd keep a persistent WebSocket connection from each online client to a stateful chat server. Um, so say we have 50 million daily active users and about 10 million concurrent connections, each server holding roughly 100,000 connections. When user A sends a message, it goes to their chat server, which looks up the recipient's connection in a presence service backed by Redis, then routes it through a Pub/Sub channel to the server that holds the recipient's socket. For offline users, we persist the message and send a push notification through APNs or FCM, and when they reconnect the client syncs everything after its last seen message ID. For ordering, global order is unnecessary and expensive. So I want per-conversation ordering, using a monotonically increasing sequence number per channel, or a Snowflake ID, assigned by the server, not trusting client clocks. Sorry, I mean not trusting client timestamps. Delivery is at-least-once with acknowledgements, and the client dedupes using an idempotency key. For storage, a write-heavy workload suits Cassandra or HBase, partitioned by conversation ID with the message ID as clustering key, so recent messages sit together. Kafka sits between the servers for durability. Target end-to-end latency is under 200 milliseconds at p99.

For a distributed key-value store, think Dynamo or Cassandra style. I'd partition with consistent hashing on a ring, and use virtual nodes, say 256 per physical machine, so that data spreads evenly and adding a node only moves about 1 over N of the keys. For replication, a replication factor of 3, where each key is stored on the next three distinct nodes clockwise on the ring, ideally in different availability zones. Um, then we tune consistency with quorum reads and writes. With N equals 3, W equals 2 and R equals 2, we get R plus W greater than N, so reads see the latest write. Conflicts from concurrent writes are resolved with vector clocks, or last write wins if we accept some data loss. During a network partition, CAP theorem says we pick between consistency and availability. Dynamo picks availability, so we accept writes on the reachable side using sloppy quorum and hinted handoff, and later repair with anti-entropy using Merkle trees, plus read repair. Sorry, I mean the replicas that were cut off get fixed once the partition heals. Failure detection uses a gossip protocol. Each node stores data in an LSM tree, with a write-ahead log, memtable, and SSTables, compacted in the background. Target is single-digit millisecond p99 reads at around 100,000 QPS per node.

So, for a payment system the first thing I do is put an idempotency key on every charge request, and I store it in Postgres with a unique constraint before I call Stripe. Right, so if the mobile app retries after a timeout, we see the same key, return the stored result, and never hit the provider twice. We also pass an Idempotency-Key header to Stripe. Um, the flow is a state machine, authorized then captured then settled, and each transition is written in the same database transaction as an outbox row, so a Kafka consumer publishes events reliably. For the ledger I use double-entry bookkeeping, append-only, where all entries must sum to zero. A refund is a new set of compensating entries, never an update. Cash balances in the wallet sit in their own account with optimistic locking on a version column. Payouts go out through ACH or SEPA in nightly batches. Then every day we pull the Stripe settlement report, compare it line by line with the ledger, and send mismatches to a dead letter queue. Webhooks can arrive late or twice, so handlers are idempotent and we verify the signature. Target is p99 under 300 ms for authorization at about 2,000 TPS. Sorry, I mean 2,000 TPS at peak, not average.

So for a distributed cache I start with sizing. Say we have 50,000 QPS of reads and about 5,000 QPS of writes, so it's read heavy. If the hot working set is 200 million keys at one kilobyte each, that's about 200 GB, so I'd go with a Redis Cluster of, um, 16 shards using consistent hashing with virtual nodes. Sorry, I mean 16 shards plus one replica each, so 32 nodes total. Eviction is LRU, or approximated LFU in Redis, with the maxmemory-policy set to allkeys-lfu, because popularity is skewed and a few hot keys dominate. Right, for consistency I use cache-aside: read from the cache, and on a miss read from PostgreSQL and populate with a TTL of five minutes plus random jitter, so keys don't expire together and cause a thundering herd. On writes I update the database first and then delete the cache key rather than update it,. For stronger guarantees I tail the database binlog with Debezium and publish invalidations through Kafka. Hot keys get a small in-process cache with a short TTL, and I use request coalescing so only one caller refills a missed key. The target is p99 under 2 ms for a hit and a hit ratio above 95 percent. We watch replication lag.

So for a web crawler with billions of URLs, let's say 5 billion pages a month, that is roughly 2,000 pages per second. The core is the URL frontier. I split it into front queues for priority, using something like PageRank or change frequency, and back queues, one per host, so we can enforce politeness. Each host gets a delay, honoring robots.txt and its Crawl-delay directive,. Um, a min-heap keyed by next allowed fetch time decides which back queue to pull from. Fetchers are a fleet of workers doing async DNS resolution with a local cache, since DNS lookups hurt throughput. Right, for URL deduplication I normalize each one, then check a Bloom filter in front of a key-value store, with a false positive rate of about one percent. For content duplicates I compute a SimHash fingerprint of the page body and compare by Hamming distance, plus a SHA-256 checksum for exact copies. Raw HTML goes into S3 as WARC files at about 300 KB per page, so about 1.5 PB a month. Sorry, I mean 1.5 PB raw, roughly 500 TB after gzip. Metadata like the content hash, ETag, and last fetched time lives in Cassandra. Parsers send new links back through Kafka. We use exponential backoff on errors and avoid spider traps with a depth limit.

So for dispatch, drivers send GPS pings every four seconds over a WebSocket connection, which with 500,000 online drivers is about 125,000 writes per second. I don't put that in a regular database. I keep live locations in Redis, and I bucket the map with Uber's H3 hexagonal grid, or S2 cells, so a nearby search is just a lookup of the rider's cell and its k-ring neighbors. Right, the matching service takes a ride request, queries those cells, filters by availability, ranks by ETA from a routing engine rather than straight-line distance, and sends an offer to the best driver with a 10 second timeout. Um, to avoid double-assigning a driver, I use a distributed lock with a short lease, or an atomic compare-and-set on driver state. The service is sharded by city or by cell with consistent hashing, and Kafka carries the location and trip events. When a region gets hot, we get surge: dynamic pricing raises fares to balance supply and demand, and we split the hot cell into smaller child cells, so load spreads across more shards. Batching matches in 2 second windows with the Hungarian algorithm beats greedy. The target is p99 under 200 ms for a match. Sorry, I mean excluding the driver's response time.

So for the notification service, let's say 50 million users and a peak of 100,000 notifications per second during a flash sale. The API accepts an event, validates it, and writes to Kafka, and everything after that is asynchronous. A fan-out worker looks up the user's preferences and quiet hours in a Redis cache with DynamoDB as the source of truth, checks opt-outs, and then publishes to separate per-channel topics for push, email and SMS, so a slow SMS vendor can't block push. Right, push goes through APNs for iOS and FCM for Android, email through SES or SendGrid, and SMS through Twilio. Um, each channel worker is idempotent, using a dedupe key per notification and user, because Kafka gives us at-least-once delivery. For retries I use exponential backoff with jitter, and after five attempts the message lands in a dead letter queue. For rate limiting I use a token bucket per provider and a sliding window per user. Sorry, I mean a sliding window for the per-user limit and a token bucket for the vendor limit, since they protect different things. Delivery receipts and bounces come back through webhooks and update status. For big campaigns we shard the audience into batches of 1,000 and use priority queues so a password reset OTP beats a marketing blast. Target is p99 under 5 seconds for transactional push.
